UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

PLAINTIFF’S CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF PROCEDURAL IRREGULARITIES AND JUDICIAL ACTIONS

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine submits this Statement. The Statement places the Court’s orders, the Clerk’s entries, the submissions those orders addressed, and the dispositions that followed in one chronology. The Statement runs through October 30, 2026, the date ECF No. 108 was entered. The Statement requests no relief.

I.	SCOPE, SOURCES, AND METHOD

1.	The sources of this Statement are the docket of this action, the orders and notices entered on it, and the filings cited by ECF number. Quoted language is reproduced from the docketed document. Page citations refer to the pages of the cited docketed document. Entries that carry no ECF number are identified by date and subject.

2.	This Statement uses two defined terms. A “judicial action” is an order, notice, or docket entry made by the Court or by the Clerk. A “procedural irregularity” is a judicial action for which the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, the Local Civil Rules of this Court, and the orders on the docket supply no stated authority, or a judicial action taken outside a deadline or requirement those sources state. The Statement also identifies discrepancies between judicial descriptions of the record and the filings to which those descriptions refer. Such discrepancies are documented as record-accuracy issues, whether or not they independently constitute violations of a procedural rule. Each sequence below identifies the governing rule and states what the rule provides. Where the rule supplies no authority for the action, the Statement says so. Where the rule supplies authority, the Statement says that instead.

3.	Each sequence is presented in a fixed order: the judicial action, with its date, ECF number, and operative language; the procedural context, meaning what was pending and what the applicable rule or order required; the subsequent action, meaning what Plaintiff filed or what the Court did next; and the procedural consequence.

4.	Part II is a ledger of every judicial action entered through October 30, 2026. Parts III through IX present seven sequences drawn from that ledger. Part X states the aggregate record in numbers. Part XI lists the matters pending on October 30, 2026.

6.	The docket contains no scheduling order, no order setting an initial pretrial conference, and no order of the District Judge addressing the timing of discovery or the Rule 26(f) conference.

III.	SEQUENCE ONE: THE COMPLAINT SAYS “ONE MAN, WITHOUT A LAWYER.” THE COURT’S FIRST ORDER SAYS “HER.”

7.	On August 6, 2026, Plaintiff filed his First Amended Complaint, ECF No. 5. The pleading contains fifty-one masculine references to Plaintiff, comprising thirty uses of “his,” six of “he,” four of “him,” two of “himself,” four of “man,” three of “Mr. Ballentine,” and one each of “father” and “husband.” These references include quotations reproduced in the pleading. The identification appears at the beginning: paragraph 2 refers to “a man’s name”; paragraph 3 states “I was the plaintiff — one man, without a lawyer”; paragraph 4 refers to “everything a man would need to test it”; and paragraph 6 refers to “what that name does to a man.” ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 2–4, 6. Subsequent factual allegations repeatedly refer to Plaintiff using “he,” “him,” and “his,” including the allegations concerning Plaintiff’s prospective testimony, account history, and alleged injuries. ECF No. 5 ¶¶ 31, 33, 41, 43, 159–160, 163, 170, 172, 174–175, 178, 180, 227–228, 231, 239.

8.	On the same date, August 6, 2026, Plaintiff filed his Motion for Partial Summary Judgment under Rule 56(a), with an alternative request under Rule 56(g), concerning whether Defendant Katie Hall acted as NCMEC’s agent and within the scope of her employment when issuing the two April 22, 2026 letters. ECF No. 6. The motion contains two uses of the feminine pronoun “her,” both referring to Defendant Hall’s employment, and none referring to Plaintiff. Its supporting memorandum expressly describes Plaintiff as having provided advance notice of subpoenas “he intended to serve.” ECF No. 7 at 1. The memorandum, a declaration, and eight exhibits accompanied the motion. ECF No. 7. The Clerk docketed the motion on August 7, 2026.

9.	On August 12, 2026, District Judge Alston entered ECF No. 12. The order states that Plaintiff “filed both her Amended Complaint and her Motion for Partial Summary Judgment” on August 6, 2026. It further directs the Clerk to provide a copy “to pro se Plaintiff at her last known address.” ECF No. 12 at 1. Those are three feminine references to Plaintiff, notwithstanding the fifty-one masculine references in the operative complaint and the additional masculine reference in the memorandum supporting the motion under consideration. The order states that Defendants’ responses to the original Complaint “are not due until August 21, 2026,” concludes that the motion “is premature,” and denies it “without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time.” Id.

10.	Local Civil Rule 56(A) displaces the timing provisions of Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(b) in this District. Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) ordinarily provides fourteen calendar days for an opposing brief unless otherwise directed by the Court. ECF No. 12 issued six days after Plaintiff filed his motion and five days after the Clerk docketed it. No Defendant had filed an opposition. NCMEC’s motion to dismiss was docketed the same day as the order. ECF Nos. 10–12. On August 12, 2026, Plaintiff submitted a notice setting the motion for hearing on September 18, 2026. The Clerk docketed the notice on August 13. ECF No. 13. On August 17, 2026, the Clerk entered a notice stating that “the hearing will not be set pursuant the Order entered on 8/12/2026 denying on the Motion.” Unnumbered entry of August 17, 2026.

11.	The first order adjudicating Plaintiff’s motion referred to him as female three times despite fifty-one masculine references in the operative complaint and one in the supporting memorandum. Four references to “man” appeared within the complaint’s first six paragraphs, including Plaintiff’s express self-identification in paragraph 3. The inconsistency was not confined to an incidental passage of the order: it appeared both in the description of the filings under review and in the directive for service. The order does not establish what materials were personally reviewed before its entry. The documented discrepancy permits a reasonable observer to question whether the complaint’s opening identification of Plaintiff was consulted or verified. The Court resolved the motion on procedural timing before opposition, did not reach the agency-and-scope issue, and specified neither a date nor a triggering event for renewal. ECF No. 12 at 1.

IV.	SEQUENCE TWO: HEARINGS SET, CONFIRMED, AND TERMINATED WITHIN TWENTY-FOUR HOURS

12.	On August 20, 2026, Plaintiff filed a motion under Rule 26(d)(1) for leave to serve three limited interrogatories on NCMEC before the Rule 26(f) conference, with a memorandum and a notice of hearing. ECF Nos. 15–17. On August 25, 2026, the Clerk set that motion, together with ECF No. 26, for hearing on September 25, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. before Magistrate Judge Davis. Unnumbered entry of August 25, 2026.

13.	On September 3, 2026, Plaintiff filed a motion under Rule 26(d)(1) for leave to serve four limited interrogatories on Meta before the Rule 26(f) conference, with a memorandum and a notice of hearing for the same date. ECF Nos. 54–56. On September 8, 2026, the Clerk set that motion for the September 25 hearing. Unnumbered entry of September 8, 2026.

14.	On August 31, 2026, Plaintiff moved for leave to appear remotely at the September 25 hearing. The motion identified ECF No. 15 and ECF No. 26. ECF No. 41.

15.	On September 8, 2026, Plaintiff withdrew ECF No. 26 and requested vacatur of the September 25 hearing “as to ECF No. 26 Only.” ECF Nos. 57–58. On September 9, 2026, Magistrate Judge Davis entered ECF No. 62. The order treats ECF No. 26 as withdrawn, vacates the hearing “solely with respect to Dkt. No. 26,” and states: “All other pending motions scheduled for September 25, 2026 at 10:00 AM in Courtroom 301 will remain as scheduled.” ECF No. 62 at 1.

16.	On the same day, Magistrate Judge Davis entered ECF No. 63. The order denies ECF No. 41 as moot on the ground that “oral argument as to Plaintiff’s Withdrawn Motion [Dkt. No. 26] is not necessary.” The order then terminates the September 25 hearing on ECF No. 15: “The undersigned deems a Motion hearing is not necessary and will resolve Plaintiff’s Interrogatories Motion on the papers.” ECF No. 63 at 1. ECF No. 41 had identified ECF No. 15 as well as ECF No. 26. ECF No. 41.

17.	On September 10, 2026, Magistrate Judge Davis entered ECF No. 65. The order terminates the September 25 hearing on ECF No. 54 on the same stated ground and sets Meta’s response for September 17 and Plaintiff’s reply for September 23. ECF No. 65 at 1.

18.	Local Civil Rule 7(J) provides that the Court may rule upon motions without an oral hearing. Rule 78(b) provides the same. Those provisions supply authority for disposition on the papers. No rule addresses an order that confirms a hearing as remaining scheduled and a second order entered the same day that terminates it.

19.	The hearing on ECF No. 15 was confirmed and terminated on September 9, 2026. The hearing on ECF No. 54 was terminated on September 10, 2026. Both motions remained pending for written disposition until October 7, 2026. ECF Nos. 62, 63, 65, 84.

V.	SEQUENCE THREE: A COMPARISON REQUIREMENT WITH NO RULE SOURCE, A TWO-DAY DEADLINE, AND ENFORCEMENT WHILE OBJECTIONS WERE PENDING

20.	On September 8, 2026, Plaintiff’s motion for leave to file a Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint was docketed with the complete proposed pleading, a declaration, a memorandum, and a notice of waiver of oral argument. ECF Nos. 59–61. The motion states: “The First Amended Complaint (ECF No. 5) is the operative pleading. The proposed SAC replaces the First Amended Complaint with one integrated pleading.” ECF No. 59 ¶ 3. The motion was submitted on the ordinary briefing schedule of Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1). ECF No. 59 ¶ 14.

21.	On September 9, 2026, Magistrate Judge Davis entered ECF No. 64. The order states that the Court “does not possess sufficient information to issue an Order on this matter.” The order directs: “Plaintiff must provide a redlined version of the Amended Complaint [Dkt. Nos. 59-1, 60-1], no later than September 11, 2026. This redlined version of the Amended Complaint must clearly indicate the changes, deletions, and additions that were made to Plaintiff’s Complaint [Dkt. No. 1].” ECF No. 64 at 1.

22.	Rule 15(a)(2) provides that a party may amend with the court’s leave and that “[t]he court should freely give leave when justice so requires.” Rule 15 contains no comparison requirement. The Local Civil Rules of this Court contain no rule numbered 15; the civil rules proceed from Local Civil Rule 7.1 to Local Civil Rule 16. No Local Civil Rule requires a redlined comparison with a motion to amend. ECF No. 64 cites no rule, no standing order, and no authority for the requirement it imposes. ECF No. 64 at 1.

23.	The comparison ordered was against the original Complaint, ECF No. 1. Plaintiff had amended that pleading as a matter of course on August 6, 2026. ECF No. 5. The motion before the Court identified ECF No. 5 as the operative pleading. ECF No. 59 ¶ 3. The order directed a comparison against the pleading ECF No. 5 had replaced. ECF No. 64 at 1.

24.	The deadline was September 11, 2026, two calendar days after entry. Plaintiff is not a registered CM/ECF user, has not consented to electronic service, and receives the Court’s orders by mail at a commercial mail-receiving agency. ECF No. 68-1 ¶ 3. Plaintiff first learned of ECF Nos. 62 through 65 at approximately 9:09 p.m. Eastern Time on September 11, 2026, through a CourtListener alert. ECF No. 68-1 ¶ 8. As of September 13, 2026, no mailed copy of ECF No. 62, 63, 64, or 65 had arrived at Plaintiff’s address of record. ECF No. 68-1 ¶ 10.

25.	On September 14, 2026, Plaintiff filed Rule 72(a) objections to ECF Nos. 63, 64, and 65, a motion to set aside ECF No. 64 and suspend its enforcement, and a memorandum with the declaration. ECF Nos. 66–68. Rule 72(a) provides that “[t]he district judge in the case must consider timely objections and modify or set aside any part of the order that is clearly erroneous or is contrary to law.”

26.	On September 18, 2026, NCMEC and Hall opposed the amendment motion. ECF No. 74. On September 22, 2026, Meta opposed it. ECF No. 83. On September 22, 2026, the Court accepted Plaintiff’s supplemental submission as a reply to ECF No. 74. ECF No. 82 at 1.

27.	On October 7, 2026, Magistrate Judge Davis entered ECF No. 84. The order states: “Plaintiff was given ample opportunity to comply with the Court’s September 9, 2026 Order [Dkt. No. 64] by producing a redlined Second Amended Complaint but has failed to do so as of the date of this Order.” The order denies ECF No. 59 on that ground. ECF No. 84 at 2. The order does not address the proposed pleading’s allegations. The order does not address ECF Nos. 66 and 67. ECF No. 84.

28.	On October 7, 2026, the objections and the motion to set aside ECF No. 64 had been pending before the District Judge for twenty-three days. On October 30, 2026, they had been pending for forty-six days. The docket contains no disposition of ECF No. 66 or ECF No. 67. Docket entries through October 30, 2026.

29.	The proposed Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint has not been accepted for filing. The order denying it rests on a requirement that no rule states, that was imposed with a two-day deadline, and that was enforced while objections to it were pending and undecided. ECF Nos. 64, 66, 67, 84.

VI.	SEQUENCE FOUR: PRE-CONFERENCE DISCOVERY DENIED FOR WANT OF AN ORDER THE RULE AUTHORIZES THE COURT TO ENTER

30.	ECF Nos. 15 and 54 each sought leave under Rule 26(d)(1) to serve a limited number of interrogatories before the Rule 26(f) conference. ECF Nos. 15, 54. NCMEC and Hall opposed ECF No. 15. ECF Nos. 33, 46. Meta opposed ECF No. 54. ECF No. 73. Plaintiff replied to each. ECF Nos. 36, 52, 81. Both motions were fully briefed.

31.	On October 7, 2026, ECF No. 84 denied both motions “as premature.” The order states: “The Court interprets these Motions as requests for expedited discovery concerning Defendants National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (‘NCMEC’) and Meta Platforms, Inc., respectively. At this time, the Court cannot issue an order concerning Plaintiff’s Motions because discovery has not officially begun in this case. Pursuant to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, discovery officially begins when the District Judge issues a Scheduling Order and currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case.” ECF No. 84 at 1–2.

32.	Rule 26(d)(1) provides: “A party may not seek discovery from any source before the parties have conferred as required by Rule 26(f), except in a proceeding exempted from initial disclosure under Rule 26(a)(1)(B), or when authorized by these rules, by stipulation, or by court order.” The rule authorizes discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference “by court order.” Each motion asked for that order. ECF Nos. 15, 54. The order states that the Court “cannot issue an order” because discovery had not begun. ECF No. 84 at 1. The rule’s text supplies the authority the order states the Court lacked. The order cites no provision of the Federal Rules for the proposition that discovery “officially begins when the District Judge issues a Scheduling Order.” ECF No. 84 at 1–2.

33.	The stated ground of denial was the absence of a scheduling order. ECF No. 84 at 2. On October 7, 2026, no scheduling order had issued. Sequence Five addresses the deadline for that order. Sequence Seven addresses what the Court did when Plaintiff moved for it.

VII.	SEQUENCE FIVE: THE SCHEDULING-ORDER DEADLINE PASSED WITHOUT AN ORDER OR A GOOD-CAUSE FINDING

34.	NCMEC and Meta were served on July 31, 2026. ECF Nos. 3, 4. NCMEC first appeared on August 12, 2026, by filing its motion to dismiss. ECF Nos. 10, 11. Meta appeared on August 21, 2026. ECF No. 21. Hall appeared on September 2, 2026. ECF No. 45.

35.	Rule 16(b)(2) provides: “The judge must issue the scheduling order as soon as practicable, but unless the judge finds good cause for delay, the judge must issue it within the earlier of 90 days after any defendant has been served with the complaint or 60 days after any defendant has appeared.” Local Civil Rule 16(B) provides that “not later than sixty (60) days from first appearance or ninety (90) days after service of the complaint, the Court shall enter an order fixing the cut-off dates for the respective parties to complete the processes of discovery, the date for a final pretrial conference and, whenever practicable, the trial date.”

36.	Sixty days after NCMEC’s first appearance was Sunday, October 11, 2026. Monday, October 12, 2026, was Columbus Day, a legal holiday under Rule 6(a)(6)(A). Under Rule 6(a)(1)(C), the period ran through Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Ninety days after service on NCMEC and Meta was October 29, 2026. The earlier of the two dates was October 13, 2026.

37.	No scheduling order issued on or before October 13, 2026. No scheduling order issued on or before October 29, 2026. No order on the docket finds good cause for delay. Docket entries through October 30, 2026.

38.	No Local Civil Rule provides that a scheduling order or a Rule 26(f) conference is deferred while a motion to dismiss is pending. Local Civil Rules 7, 16, and 26.

VIII.	SEQUENCE SIX: A FINANCIAL-INTEREST APPLICATION, A REASSIGNMENT, AND A MOOTNESS ORDER SIGNED BY THE JUDGE WHOSE INTEREST WAS AT ISSUE

39.	On October 13, 2026, Plaintiff moved under 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) and § 455(a) for the disqualification of Magistrate Judge Davis and for priority determination. ECF No. 86. The motion attached Magistrate Judge Davis’s financial disclosure reports for calendar years 2024 and 2025. Each report identifies “FB common stock” at Part VII, line 6, with no transaction reported on that line. ECF No. 86 at 2; ECF Nos. 86-2, 86-3. The motion states that “FB” was the Nasdaq trading symbol for the Class A common stock of Facebook, Inc., which changed its name to Meta Platforms, Inc. on October 28, 2021. ECF No. 86 at 2–3.

40.	The motion requested that the Court state on the record: whether the reported asset is common stock of Meta Platforms, Inc.; whether the interest was held on July 30, 2026, and on each date on which ECF Nos. 62, 63, 64, 65, 82, and 84 were entered; the date and manner of any divestiture; whether the interest was held directly or through a fund within 28 U.S.C. § 455(d)(4)(i); and any fact material to 28 U.S.C. § 455(f). ECF No. 86 at 4–5. The motion stated that it “alleges no bias, hostility, improper motive, bad faith, or intentional nondisclosure” and “rests on two signed financial disclosure reports and the docket.” ECF No. 86 at 2.

41.	Section 455(b)(4) provides that a magistrate judge “shall also disqualify himself” where “[h]e knows that he, individually or as a fiduciary, or his spouse or minor child residing in his household, has a financial interest in the subject matter in controversy or in a party to the proceeding.” Section 455(e) provides that no magistrate judge “shall accept from the parties to the proceeding a waiver of any ground for disqualification enumerated in subsection (b).” Section 455(f) permits a judge who learns of a financial interest after “substantial judicial time has been devoted to the matter” to continue if the interest is divested.

42.	On October 22, 2026, the Clerk entered: “Case Reassigned to Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick. Magistrate Judge Ivan D. Davis no longer assigned to the case.” Unnumbered entry of October 22, 2026. The entry identifies no order, no request, and no assignment procedure as the source of the reassignment.

43.	On October 22, 2026, Magistrate Judge Davis signed ECF No. 96. The order states: “ORDERED that Plaintiff’s Motion is DENIED AS MOOT. The case has been reassigned to Magistrate Judge William E. Fitzpatrick.” ECF No. 96 at 1. The order makes no finding on whether the reported asset is Meta common stock, whether it was held on July 30, 2026, or on any date on which ECF Nos. 62, 63, 64, 65, 82, or 84 were entered, whether it was divested, or how it was held. ECF No. 96.

44.	Reassignment addresses future participation. ECF Nos. 62, 63, 64, 65, 82, and 84 were entered before reassignment. ECF No. 84 denied amendment and denied discovery directed to Meta. The question whether the magistrate judge held Meta common stock when those orders were entered was presented in ECF No. 86 and is not answered in ECF No. 96. ECF No. 86 at 4–5; ECF No. 96 at 1.

45.	On October 23, 2026, Plaintiff filed Rule 72(a) objections to ECF No. 96 and a motion to set aside or modify that order, determine reassignment authority, and supplement ECF No. 93. ECF Nos. 97–99. The docket contains no disposition of either. Docket entries through October 30, 2026.

IX.	SEQUENCE SEVEN: SCHEDULING AND RULE 26(f) MOTIONS DENIED THE DAY THEY WERE DOCKETED, ON THE AUTHORITY OF A DISTRICT-JUDGE DECISION THAT APPEARS ON NO DOCKET ENTRY

46.	On October 28, 2026, Plaintiff filed a motion for entry of a scheduling order and, as necessary, an initial pretrial conference, and a separate motion for an order directing completion of the Rule 26(f) conference and submission of a discovery plan. ECF Nos. 103, 105. Each motion was accompanied by a memorandum. ECF Nos. 104, 106. A declaration with exhibits accompanied the Rule 26(f) motion. ECF No. 107. The Clerk docketed the motions on October 29, 2026.

47.	Rule 26(f)(1) provides that “the parties must confer as soon as practicable—and in any event at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is to be held or a scheduling order is due under Rule 16(b).” Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) provides fourteen calendar days for an opposing brief.

48.	On October 29, 2026, the day the motions were docketed, Magistrate Judge Fitzpatrick signed ECF No. 108. The Clerk entered the order on October 30, 2026. No Defendant had filed an opposition. The fourteen-day period had not run. ECF No. 108; docket entries of October 28 through October 30, 2026.

49.	ECF No. 108 identifies four forms of relief sought: a scheduling order; an order directing completion of the Rule 26(f) conference and filing of discovery plans; an initial pretrial conference; and, if any step were postponed, a statement of the date or event on which scheduling would next be addressed. ECF No. 108 at 1. The order states that three motions to dismiss are pending, quotes a District of Maryland decision for the proposition that courts commonly wait for resolution of preliminary motions before entering a Rule 16 order, and then states: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss. Accordingly, Plaintiff’s Motions (Dkts. 103, 105) are DENIED without prejudice.” ECF No. 108 at 2.

50.	The District Judge has entered five orders and notices in this action: ECF No. 12 (denying partial summary judgment as premature), ECF No. 25 (notice of the right to respond to a motion to dismiss), ECF No. 48 (same), ECF No. 50 (vacating a hearing and directing decision on the papers), and ECF No. 70 (granting leave to file a sur-reply). None addresses discovery. None addresses the Rule 26(f) conference. None addresses the timing of a scheduling order. ECF Nos. 12, 25, 48, 50, 70.

51.	The statement that “discovery officially begins when the District Judge issues a Scheduling Order” appears in ECF No. 84, an order of the Magistrate Judge. ECF No. 84 at 1–2. ECF No. 108 identifies no docket entry, date, or order as the source of the decision it attributes to the District Judge. ECF No. 108 at 2.

52.	ECF No. 108 contains no finding of good cause for delay under Rule 16(b)(2). ECF No. 108 does not state the date or event on which scheduling will next be addressed, the fourth form of relief it identifies. ECF No. 108 at 1–2.

53.	On October 7, 2026, discovery was denied because no scheduling order existed. ECF No. 84 at 1–2. On October 29, 2026, the motion for a scheduling order was denied because the District Judge had chosen to defer discovery. ECF No. 108 at 2. The docket contains no order of the District Judge making that choice. Docket entries through October 30, 2026.
